newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader moves to end row with parliament.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader moves to end row with parliament.

text.p: Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko offered an olive branch to his political opponents on Saturday in a bid to end a bitter row with parliament which has been raging for two months.

"I declare here today, that I am ready for compromise today, right now, on grounds of principle, and not as a result of haggling with political extremists," Lukashenko told an "All- Belarus People's Congress" he had convened.
Lukashenko, 42, and parliament each want to hold their own referendum to propose conflicting constitutional amendments which would rob the other of their authority.

A majority of deputies has twice voted to hold a vote on a parliamentary republic -- with no president -- on November 24. Lukashenko wanted a December 7 referendum on proposals to give him more power and extend his stay in office.

Lukashenko, who according to the constitution must get parliament's approval for a referendum date, on Saturday declared in a speech broadcast live on television and radio that he had changed his mind.
"I decided yesterday, and am asking for your agreement today, to hold (my) referendum on November 24," he said.
"If we are together, we can win on November 24, and on December 24, and on January 24," Lukashenko added.
Thousands of protesters had gathered in central Minsk earlier on Saturday to demand Lukashenko's resignation, accusing him of running a dictatorship.
The largely nationalist crowd was furious with his policies, which favour a closer union with Russia, and with his derisive comments about the little-used Belarussian language.
"Down with Lukashenko!" and "Long Live Belarus!" they cried as they headed for a meeting to hear opposition leaders.
A smaller crowd of about 3,000 later tried to reach the Palace of Sport where the congress was being held, but were eventually dispersed without major incident by riot police.
Previous such demonstrations have ended with violence and in some cases, scores of arrests.
It seemed unlikely that Lukashenko's compromise would win the hearts of his opponents but he enjoys solid support in the provinces and among local officials he appointed.

Lukashenko, supported by 58 percent of the electorate in July 1994 when he won the presidential poll on a platform of fighting corruption and re-building ties with Russia, stormed out of parliament last week and said compromise was impossible.
He said then he would turn to the people's congress for their approval of his referendum -- apparently bypassing parliament and ignoring the constitution altogether.
Lukashenko's behaviour has attracted criticism from abroad in recent weeks.
His referendum revolves around constitutional amendements which would extend his term, due to end in July 1999, by more than two years, and broaden his powers.
Social democrat leader and anti-Lukashenko deputy Stanislav Shushkevich said the compromise was a good sign but that it might not bring an end to the political struggle.
"If Lukashenko does not throw out parliament's referendum questions, then this is the start of a path to stability," he said on Saturday.
He said Lukashenko had probably felt forced to change his mind because of increasing pressure from outside Belarus.
Lukashenko's congress is due to continue on Sunday, when delegates are expected to approve his proposals.
